where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/b9/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-634f078a-6dcb-548c-8f80-dad54be93eec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-634f078a-6dcb-548c-8f80-dad54be93eec" :answer-field/id #uuid "634f078a-6dcb-548c-8f80-dad54be93eec" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-7406e360-d054-59fe-8f8f-ff8531ac1adc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-05ff21cb-9e33-53f3-b627-a88a79716c30" "answer-b9b8980a-616f-5aa2-877a-5c0ee10376d7" "answer-989f1950-08af-5b66-a148-ca15e1457577" "answer-7406e360-d054-59fe-8f8f-ff8531ac1adc" "answer-3abf3164-1e19-59b8-a518-c866ee98eb86"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05ff21cb-9e33-53f3-b627-a88a79716c30" :answer/id #uuid "05ff21cb-9e33-53f3-b627-a88a79716c30" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9b8980a-616f-5aa2-877a-5c0ee10376d7" :answer/id #uuid "b9b8980a-616f-5aa2-877a-5c0ee10376d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-989f1950-08af-5b66-a148-ca15e1457577" :answer/id #uuid "989f1950-08af-5b66-a148-ca15e1457577" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7406e360-d054-59fe-8f8f-ff8531ac1adc" :answer/id #uuid "7406e360-d054-59fe-8f8f-ff8531ac1adc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3abf3164-1e19-59b8-a518-c866ee98eb86" :answer/id #uuid "3abf3164-1e19-59b8-a518-c866ee98eb86" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176485 :question/problem "Given that

$$

$$

 we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3})\,dx+({y}^{4}+{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-(-3{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{81}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{243}{4}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{243}{4}(2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{243\text{ }\,\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176145 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176145 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186175879 :question/problem "Given that

$$

#uuid "736cedc4-b5c1-5e97-b975-c6db4fd154c1" :step/math-academy-id 35775} {:db/id 17592186176807 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177037 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](images/dd/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0b5a23c7-4ccf-5122-8b5f-98fbabb0e367" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5838 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0b3de726-ead0-5369-a1fe-3dcc61b38bbc" :step/math-academy-id 35776 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176808}} {:db/id 17592186176808 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176024 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175879 :question/id #uuid "40a301b7-9eaa-59e1-bcb0-4a35fecbff69" :question/math-academy-id "e-9551"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "695a4336-df48-56c9-8472-c2f51a496819" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049084} {:db/id 17592186051070}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176311} {:db/id 17592186176485} {:db/id 17592186262625} {:db/id 17592186262628} {:db/id 17592186262632} {:db/id 17592186405036} {:db/id 17592186405043}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "f69ccccf-5d34-5f08-95d0-7af5d0c7628b" :step/math-academy-id 35777 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176735}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Polar Coordinates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176145} {:db/id 17592186176807 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177037 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral
